Coming from someone with experience in ethical hacking, wireless security, networking, firewalls, server administration and so on, this game covers: 
- basic linux commands
- the most basic understanding of nmap (as in just the command that probes an IP lol)
- Repetitive Exploits in the form of exe files that require a port number
- Data enumeration
- Adding a Shell to a node in order to overload proxy's

Pros:
- GUI is cool to look at
- Simplifies hacking for a somewhat better understanding
- Some parts require you to actually use your brain

Cons:
- Only has a handful of linux commands
- Repetitive
- Not an accurate representation of the cyber kill chain process
- I had to create a "Settings" file with a bunch of random settings that I had to get online for the game to actually display on the screen

But the game is pretty cool.

Everything you pick up in this game comes back into play later. No features are left to dry. If you're stuck on something, go through your /bin list to see if there's somewhere else you can scan or something else you can do!
This game really encourages you to pay close attention to detail, and quite frankly that's awesome. I love it!

I wasn't quite sure what to expect with a game where the premise is you're a hacker, but needless to say whatever expectations I may have had were met and exceeded.  There are different ways to go about using the tools you have to crack into different networks--whether you rely on the UI or you're like me and like using the text commands (which are close to real commands, from my understanding)--and a very interesting look into just what could happen if you give an average joe a godly superprogram that can crack anything.

My only gripe is the story feels a little ham-fisted at times, and Project Junebug was morbidly out-of-place for the general plot, but for a general puzzler about hacking, it's good.  Definitely a good use of a day.

If you grew up on a command line, or perhaps just wondered what it might be like to live or die (or go to jail) by one, this game is pretty enthralling. I mean, sure, it takes liberties with how much can really be communicated through a command line, especially where bona fide jeopardy is concerned, but in the course of play I felt like it just plain old WORKS. It's entertaining, immersive, and rewarding, especially if you take the time to dig around in places you're not supposed to be... which is kind of the point, right? I'll admit there were a few times when I thought I had run up against developer errors instead of gameplay wrinkles, but in hindsight I can safely say that those were all on me. Play with confidence that the developer has you in the palm of his hands throughout.

Hacknet is a fantastic game that truly captures the essence of what it's like to be a hacker. The hacking simulator mechanics are incredibly well done and make the game incredibly immersive and enjoyable.

One of the things that I loved most about Hacknet was the way that it kept me coming back for more. Every time I played, I found myself getting sucked into the game world and wanting to continue hacking and uncovering new secrets.

The game's story is also really engaging, with a variety of different missions and challenges to complete. It's a game that definitely keeps you on your toes and constantly encourages you to think outside of the box.

Overall, Hacknet is an excellent game that I would highly recommend to anyone who is a fan of hacking or just enjoys a good puzzle. It's one of the best games I've played in a long time and I can't wait to see what the developers come up with next.

I do not agree with the statement of "Hacknet focuses on real hacking, not the Hollywood-style version of it." This game and it's "techniques" for "hacking" are straight out of Hollywood. There are some useful concepts, but the actual methods of "hacking" are not realistic in any way whatsoever. Reconnaissance and such are somewhat realistic and it does teach extremely basic unix commands such as cd, ls, cat, rm. But the concepts and ideas to break through SSH and ports are completely false. 

I understand this is a game and it is meant to be fun, but that is all it is. I would not recommend this if you think it is going to be able to teach you much or give you a realistic sense on how penetration testing works.

This game is amazing in it's own special way. It is much more of a visual novel than a full fledged game, but the storytelling is pretty solid.

You're a small hacker wannabe and get contacted by a very prominent other hacker that had disappeared 2 weeks ago. You need to discover what went down. Pretty simple premise.
The main issue I would have with this is that the entire middle portion of the game (i.e. more than half) is just spent grinding contracts for networks to gain some cred, and while a couple stories in there are cool (I'm sorry for this one guy......), most are nothing really extraordinary and are purely as filler.
You can also look at some bash.org conversations sometimes at least... that's something, right?

When it comes to the actual gameplay... it's very repetitive, you always do the same thing with no variation and minor escalation: probe, kill proxy, kill firewall, kill ports, profit. It's not really engaging despite the first minutes where you feel like a movie hacker; you know you're not doing much, but you look cool.

Overall, very cool game! The ending really got me on the edge of my seat, surprisingly! I probably wouldn't want to replay it anytime soon (sooo repetitive blerghglglelbll), but it's a fun ride where you can pretend you know stuff about computers.

Great idea - terrible execution. For the whole duration of the game you perform same actions again, again and again. And again. Oh, and AGAIN. The totally optional Clicker mini-game and tutorial are the best and most memorable parts of it, and that's saying something.

All of this game's content can be listed as follows:
do {

*check your email, get contract details*
probe
-- Oh, heck, a proxy again.
connect xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx
shell
connect sss.sss.sss.sss
connect yyy.yyy.yyy.yyy
shell
connect sss.sss.sss.sss
connect zzz.zzz.zzz.zzz
shell
connect sss.sss.sss.sss
connect... -- nah, that's probably enough, I still need to "hack" that firewall.
*overloading proxy*
analyze
analyze
analyze
analyze
analyze
*Proxy bypassed*
analyze
analyze
analyze
analyze
solve XXXXXXX
WebServerWorm 80
SMTPoverflow 25
FTPbounce 21
SSHcrack 22
*waiting until the end of it*
porthack
*waiting again*
-- Finally.
*doing same repeatative stuff on the hacked machine, clear logs, disconnect*

} while true;

And that's about it. You don't even have to think. At all. More than that, you actually CAN'T think to improve something in your game. Everything you do here is just following instructions like a machine. Bypass Propxy, solve Firewall, open ports, hack ports, get data, clear logs, disconnect, rinse and repeat. Since I didn't actually finish the game, I guess there will be more "hacking tools" introduced, but it won't change anything. The core of the game stays the same - just mindless repetition. This has nothing to do with actual cybersecurity business.

The moral side of some contracts is also questionable, to say the least. They want you to:
- get a private medical card of a person (for the sake of curiosity of some idiot forum-dweller);
- forge a degree for some "ally guy" of the (illegal) group you're working for.
- bring the secret [strike]KFC[/strike]CFC spice recepie out to the public, just, you know, for fun;
And that's only what I've encountered so far.

Some of the more "officially looking" contracts also make little sense. Like the one given to you by a high school administration, where you need to get IT admin password, so the administration can personally investigate a suspicion of IT department sharing student's emails data with outsiders (presumably, student's parents). It's so ridiculously stupid it could actually be another (one of many) dev's attempt at humour.


A word of advice:
If you suddenly became interested in all this "terminal net graph hacker cool" thing, just get VMWare\Oracle, download some Linux distros and build your own virtual network to play with. Way more fun, inherently legal and educative way of spending hours upon hours of your time typing stuff in CLI.
